extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, undergraduate mathematics instructors, and teacher-educators
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating prospective mathematics teachers' geometric reasoning using Usiskin's 25-item van Hiele test and related analyses (pre/post design, scalogram, VHL assignment rules). Also documents how professional mathematicians use diagrams when constructing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph usage purposes (six categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants used the graph for six purposes: (a) noticing properties and generating conjectures of the sine function; (b) representing or instantiating an assertion or an idea on the graph; (c) disconfirming conjectures that are not true; (d) verifying properties that they deduced through logic; (e) suggesting proving techniques (such as using the periodicity of the sine function or forming a case-based argument) to prove the theorem; (f) using the graphs as a justification for claims they wished to make (e.g., noting that a student could see that a claim was true by inspecting the graph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories can be used as analytic codes or as desiderata when teaching students to use diagrams: check whether a diagram is being used to generate conjectures, represent assertions, falsify conjectures, verify logically deduced properties, suggest proof approaches, or as visual justification. The study notes variation among mathematicians in which purposes they used and that some produced proofs not based on graph-derived inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference source coding
rubrics_metrics.description: For each inference made while constructing a proof, code whether the inference was made from inspecting the appearance of the graph, from a logical deduction from some other inference, from recall, or from some other source (e.g., a metaphor, some other diagram).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also record what previous inferences the new inference was based upon and whether the inference became part of the chain of argumentation that led to the final written proof. This is both an analytic rubric for research and a diagnostic tool for evaluating how diagram-based reasoning translates into formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain-of-argument inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine for each coded inference whether it was part of a chain of argumentation that led to the final written proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to distinguish inferences that influenced the final proof from those that were exploratory or discarded. The paper found many inferences/suggested approaches that did not appear in the final proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skills needed to translate graphical inferences into formal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Identified skills include access to domain-specific proving strategies (e.g., knowledge that for continuous functions proving injectivity and monotonicity are equivalent), fluency in algebraic manipulations, and the ability to translate logical statements into equivalent statements that are easier to work with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These skills are listed as prerequisites or evaluative criteria for successful use of diagrams in proof construction; instructors should teach and assess these alongside diagram use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion (or omission) of diagrams in final proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one participant included the diagram in the proof he would present in the textbook, illustrating that formal presentations often omit the informal processes (diagrams) used to create proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phenomenon is important pedagogically: evaluate whether students can explicate informal diagram-based reasoning even when their final written proof omits the diagram; consider teaching students to include or explicitly reference diagrams to make informal reasoning transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of graphs to suggest proving techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphs can suggest specific proving techniques (e.g., using periodicity of sine, forming case-based arguments, calculus-based derivative arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or teaching proof construction, note whether students leverage the graph to select an appropriate proof strategy and whether they can justify why that technique is applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Van Hiele Level 1 — Visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Visualization - students visualize geometrical figures as a whole and recognize them by their particular shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This level is characterized by recognition of shapes, not analysis of properties or relationships. Behavioral checklists and test items corresponding to questions 1–5 (Usiskin's test) assess this level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Van Hiele Level 2 — Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis - students recognize the geometric properties of the different figures and are able to analyze the figures separately, but do not yet make connections between figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test items for this level probe identification and isolation of properties within a single figure (Usiskin questions 6–10 correspond to this level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Van Hiele Level 3 — Abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstraction - students recognize relationships between figures and between properties of different figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At this level students begin to see relationships and can work across figures; Usiskin's items for this level assess those behaviors (questions 11–15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Van Hiele Level 4 — Formal deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal deduction - students can write proofs and should provide justifications for each step in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This level expects students to produce reasoned, stepwise proofs with justification for steps. Usiskin's test items for this level (questions 16–20) and classroom tasks emphasizing proof-writing target this level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Van Hiele Level 5 — Rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor - 'student understands the formal aspect of deduction… [and] should understand the role and necessity of indirect proof and proof by contrapositive' and students can understand non-Euclidean geometries (quoted from Mayberry, 1983).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highest level involves meta-understanding of proof methods and alternative geometrical frameworks; test items (questions 21–25) and advanced tasks probe this capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usiskin 25-item test: level assignment rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Usiskin's 25-item test groups five questions per van Hiele level (questions 1–5 → VHL 1, 6–10 → VHL 2, etc.). To assign a participant to level n, at least four items must have been answered correctly at level n and at each preceding level. If a participant answered fewer than four questions correctly at level 1, then level 0 was assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors used the '4-item criterion' because random guessing was not expected and a higher mastery level was expected for participants who had completed high school geometry. Use this explicit scoring rule to convert raw responses into a classical van Hiele level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raw scoring and VHL interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participant is assigned a raw score (out of 25) and a classical van Hiele level based on the 4-item criterion; groups of five questions correspond to successive levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For program evaluation, interpret both raw-score changes (pre/post) and level changes, with particular attention to levels associated with proof (levels 4 and 5). The study presents both raw-score means and VHL summaries by group and gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument selection criteria (practical validity/tradeoffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Usiskin's test was chosen because it is quicker (timed to 35 minutes), more convenient, and shorter than alternatives (e.g., RUMEUS, Mayberry's 128-item test), and prior work confirmed its validity for similar populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting an assessment instrument, weigh tradeoffs between depth and practicality: a shorter, validated instrument may be preferable in classroom settings even if a more comprehensive instrument exists. Document limitations and rationale for choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of hierarchical structure via scalogram (Guttman) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Before interpreting pre/post results, implement a Guttman scalogram analysis (as in Mayberry, 1983) to determine whether the van Hiele test operates as a hierarchy for the participant sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scalogram results to justify treating test levels as hierarchical; the authors report that the scalogram analysis implied Usiskin's test operated adequately for their participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre/post test design and analysis by VHL
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a pre- and posttest design to assess course influence on van Hiele levels; analyze raw scores and changes by VHL, with specific attention to proof-related levels (4 and 5) and subgroup differences (e.g., by gender).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study reports separate analyses for two cohorts, summarizes means and VHL distributions, and highlights statistically significant gains at specific levels for females (VHL 4) and males (VHL 5) in respective data sets.
